title: Madhya Pradesh Becomes Fourth Indian State to Pass Uniform Civil Code
excerpt: The 120-page legislation bans polygamy, mandates registration of marriages and live-in relationships, and grants equal inheritance rights to sons and daughters. The bill now awaits the Governor's assent.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Madhya Pradesh's cabinet approved the UCC Bill-2026, set for introduction in the Assembly on July 20.
  • The bill bans polygamy and imposes penalties for undisclosed live-in relationships, up to five years in prison.
  • Scheduled Tribes are exempt from the UCC, simplifying succession laws from 100 clauses to 30.
  • If passed by July 25, Madhya Pradesh will be India's second state to implement a Uniform Civil Code.

  • Madhya Pradesh Assembly passed the UCC Bill on July 21, becoming the fourth state after Uttarakhand, Gujarat, and Assam to adopt a uniform civil code.
  • The law bans polygamy, triple talaq, and nikah halala, and makes registration of marriages, divorces, and live-in relationships compulsory.
  • Sons and daughters get equal inheritance rights; married men entering live-in relationships face up to five years in prison.
  • Scheduled Tribes are exempted from the code's provisions; the bill now awaits the Governor's assent.

BHOPAL — The Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly on Tuesday passed the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill 2026 amid heated opposition protests, making the state the fourth in India to adopt such legislation after Uttarakhand, Gujarat, and Assam.

The bill, a 120-page document drafted by a seven-member committee headed by former Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai, seeks to create a common civil law governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and live-in relationships across all communities in the state.

Four Pillars of the Code

Presenting the legislation in the Assembly, Chief Minister Mohan Yadav described the UCC's framework as resting on "four pillars" — marriage, divorce, succession, and live-in relationships. He said religious ceremonies, rituals, traditions, and customs would continue without interference.

Key Provisions of the UCC Bill
›Bans polygamy across all religions.
›Mandates registration of live-in relationships.
›Exempts Scheduled Tribes from UCC provisions.
›Simplifies succession laws significantly.
https://x.com/TheMuslim786/status/2079866301674328544

The code sets the minimum marriage age at 21 for men and 18 for women, applies a blanket ban on polygamy regardless of religion, and makes marriage registration compulsory. Failure to register a marriage will attract a fine. Divorces can now take place only through legal proceedings.

"Daughters and sons will have equal rights in the ancestral property. Legally, the women's property will also be transferred in the same manner as that of men. This is a right to equality for mothers and sisters."

— Mohan Yadav, Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh

The bill also criminalises instant triple talaq and nikah halala. Live-in relationships must be registered with the government within one month of their commencement. If either partner is below 21, the registrar is required to inform parents or guardians and notify the local police station. Children born from live-in relationships will be granted legal status, and a woman deserted by her live-in partner will have the right to seek maintenance.

A married man who deceives his wife and enters a live-in relationship faces up to five years in prison — one of the strictest such provisions among the states that have adopted a UCC.

Exemptions and Consultations

The code exempts Scheduled Tribes and communities protected under Articles 342 and 366(25) of the Constitution from its provisions. Yadav said the government collected over 1,164 public suggestions during the drafting process and claimed 93 percent citizen support for the legislation. The state studied the UCC models adopted by Uttarakhand, Gujarat, and Assam before finalising its own version.

![Madhya Pradesh. Key Takeaways Madhya Pradesh's cabinet approved the UCC Bill-2026, set for introduction in the Assembly on July 20.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/68/India-5749_-_Visvanatha_Temple_-_Flickr_-_archer10_%28Dennis%29.jpg)

Opposition Protests

The bill's passage was far from smooth. Congress legislators demanded the legislation be referred to a Select Committee for detailed scrutiny. Leader of the Opposition Umang Singhar, along with MLAs Atif Aqueel and Arif Masood, argued that minority rights under Article 29 of the Constitution should be safeguarded and accused the ruling BJP of pursuing a political agenda.

Congress MLAs entered the well of the House and raised slogans against the bill, forcing proceedings to be adjourned twice. Singhar argued that the state had more pressing priorities, particularly the long-pending demand for 27 percent reservation for Other Backward Classes. Despite the disruptions, Speaker Narendra Singh Tomar continued proceedings and declared the bill passed.

What Comes Next

The bill now awaits the Governor's assent before it can be enacted into law. Chief Minister Yadav has directed BJP legislators to explain the code's provisions to constituents, framing it as a historic step toward fulfilling the directive principle enshrined in Article 44 of the Constitution, which calls upon states to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens.

"No one will be able to enter into arbitrary marriages and divorces outside the jurisdiction of the court."

— Mohan Yadav, Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh

For the Indian diaspora, the legislation carries direct implications for property inheritance. Under the new code, daughters — including those residing abroad — would have equal rights to ancestral property in Madhya Pradesh, aligning the state's succession laws with the push for gender parity that has gained momentum across several BJP-governed states.

With four states now having passed UCC legislation, the political debate over a nationwide uniform civil code — a longstanding BJP promise and a contentious issue across India's religious and political spectrum — is set to intensify ahead of future state elections.
